children: By Ed Frankl
The Bank of England is set to keep interest rates on hold this week, though rate-setters will likely leave the door open to more tightening as tensions in the Middle East escalate further.
Investors are also likely to focus on the continued, albeit slower, reduction of the central bank's sovereign-debt portfolio, as yields on those bonds, known as gilts, have reached multidecade highs.
The bank has maintained its key policy rate at 3.75% since December last year, at a time when policymakers were anticipating rate cuts and inflation set to decline heading into 2026.

Instead, the outbreak of the war in Iran prompted a radical upward revision of inflation forecasts, ending any chance of policy loosening. Investors now expect at least one quarter-point hike by the end of the year.

Despite the hold expected this week, economists think the bank's monetary-policy committee will strike a hawkish tone, noting that energy prices have climbed since the last policy meeting in July. Crude oil rose above $100 a barrel last week, while European natural-gas costs hit their highest since 2023.

In July, the BOE said it expected inflation to average 3.2% in the fourth quarter of the year, from 2.9% that month, taking the level of price growth further above the 2% target. The latest inflation data for August, which rate-setters will see before they make their decision, is due on Wednesday.

Energy prices aren't the only factor driving inflation. The BOE expects food inflation, which has been cooling in recent months, to reach 3.5% by the end of this year. The impact of the conflict on food has been exacerbated by heatwaves in Europe, with concerns also mounting over the developing El Nino weather phenomenon. Speaking to lawmakers last week, Bank of England Gov. Andrew Bailey said the balance of inflation risks remain to the upside.
Even if the monetary-policy committee's guidance remains non-committal, it is expected to say it stands ready to act.
However, the majority of policymakers continue to see little evidence of second-round effects, such as those that feed into increased wages, a factor that could prompt a cycle of ever higher prices.
That gives policymakers "breathing space to sit back and see how things play out", Oxford Economics chief U.K. economist Andrew Goodwin said in a note.

"We don't expect material second-round effects to emerge, largely because labor-market conditions are much looser than they were in 2022. So we expect the MPC to hold [the policy] rate at 3.75% until well into next year," he added.
The recent rise in gilt yields--effectively the interest rate on government bonds--has also been read as performing policy tightening without the bank having had to raise the bank's rates.

The U.K. last week sold long-dated 30-year bonds with the highest yield since 1998, while the more closely watched 10-year bond has a yield near highs since 2008. Rising yields also push mortgages and corporate-borrowing costs upward, squeezing the flow of money into the economy.
Like other economies, British bond yields have climbed in recent months as investors fret about growing government debt loads and the persistence of inflation as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed.
According to the BOE's July survey of market participants, investors expect the reduction of its bond portfolio--known as quantitative tightening--to slow in the coming year.
Those gilts were mostly acquired in the years following the global financial crisis under a program known as quantitative easing intended to stimulate the economy and boost inflation.

In the 12 months through this month, the BOE has reduced its holdings by 70 billion pounds, equivalent to $94.84 billion, through a combination of letting bonds mature and sales. Neither the Federal Reserve nor the European Central Bank have used sales to shrink their bondholdings.

Investors pencil in 50 billion pounds in quantitative tightening for the year ahead. Since it started its QT program in 2022, the bank has shrunk its gilts portfolio to 488 billion pounds from 895 billion pounds.
